title: Finite separated Noetherian scheme cover of a separated Noetherian algebraic space
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $X$ be an algebraic space over $\operatorname{Spec}K$ [def-trf-algebraic-space, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Assume $X$ is Noetherian and separated over $K$, meaning its relative diagonal is a closed immersion on scheme tests [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Locally Noetherian means that an etale scheme atlas is locally Noetherian [pqf-def-locnoeth]; Noetherian means locally Noetherian, quasi-compact, and quasi-separated. Quasi-compact means that every open cover has a finite subcover, and quasi-separated means that the diagonal is quasi-compact on scheme tests. There exist a Noetherian scheme $U$, separated over $K$ [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-proper-morphism], and a finite surjective morphism $f:U\to X$ over $K$. Surjectivity means surjectivity on field-valued point classes [def-a1-space-point-topology]. A morphism of algebraic spaces is finite if every base change by a scheme is represented by a finite morphism of schemes [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism].

source.place: Tag 09YC (proposition-there-is-a-scheme-finite-over), clause (1); the separated Noetherian source follows from Tags 04NZ (spaces-morphisms, lemma-finite-proper) and 04ZK (spaces-morphisms, lemma-locally-finite-type-locally-noetherian).

proof.text: Because $X$ is Noetherian, it is quasi-compact and quasi-separated over $S=\operatorname{Spec}K$. It is then also quasi-separated in the absolute sense used by the integral-cover lemma: $\Delta_{X/\mathbf Z}$ is $\Delta_{X/K}$ followed by $X\times_KX\to X\times_{\mathbf Z}X$, the base change of the diagonal $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}(K\otimes_{\mathbf Z}K)$, which is a closed immersion because multiplication $K\otimes_{\mathbf Z}K\to K$ is surjective; closed immersions are quasi-compact and composites of quasi-compact maps are quasi-compact. Apply the integral-cover lemma over $S$ to obtain an $S$-scheme $Y$ and an integral surjection $p:Y\to X$. No finiteness assertion about $Y$ is being assumed.

Apply integral approximation to $p:Y\to X$. It gives a small nonempty directed inverse system $(Y_i\to X)$ of finite finitely presented maps, with qcqs stages, affine transitions, and limit $Y$. The preceding step supplies exactly the integral map and qcqs target required by this lemma. This is also a limit over $S$: for compatible $S$-maps $W\to Y_i$, directedness makes their composites to $X$ equal (compare any two through a common later stage). They therefore form a cone over that single map $W\to X$, so the limit property over $X$ gives a unique $S$-map $W\to Y$. For uniqueness, any other such S-map has the same composite to X after composing with one projection (the index set is nonempty), and is therefore the same X-map by the slice limit property.

The limit $Y$ is a scheme. The schematic-stage lemma therefore gives $i$ for which $U=Y_i$ is a scheme. Let $f:U\to X$ be its finite finitely presented structure map. It is surjective: for a point class $x$ of $X$, lift it to a field-valued point class $y$ of $Y$ using $p$, and take its image under $p_i:Y\to Y_i$; its image under $f$ is $x$, since $f\circ p_i=p$. This argument does not require $p_i$ itself to be surjective.

source.place: Tag 09YC(1), schematic stage via Tag 07SR; surjectivity from the factorization of p

proof.text: The finite-presentation property of $f$ includes local finite presentation on etale charts. Apply the locally-Noetherian conclusion of the space cotangent-coherence lemma to $f$, with locally Noetherian target $X$: $U$ admits a surjective etale cover $\{T_a\to U\}$ by schemes $T_a$ with affine open covers by spectra of Noetherian rings, i.e. locally Noetherian schemes. As $U$ is a scheme, each $T_a\to U$ is an etale morphism of schemes and the family is a jointly surjective etale covering, so the etale descent lemma for local Noetherianness makes the scheme $U$ locally Noetherian. Only the first conclusion of the cotangent lemma is used; no cotangent-complex identification is needed. Local finite presentation is available from the approximation, without assuming that an arbitrary finite map is finitely presented.

source.place: Tag 04ZK (lemma-locally-finite-type-locally-noetherian); here finite presentation supplies the stronger hypothesis of the existing DAG lemma

proof.text: Choose a surjective etale map $T\to X$ with $T$ a quasi-compact scheme, using the atlas criterion for quasi-compactness. The pullback $V=U\times_XT$ is a scheme finite over $T$ by the scheme-test definition of finiteness. The affine opens of $T$ form an open cover by the definition of a scheme; quasi-compactness selects finitely many. Their inverse images in $V$ are affine because the finite scheme morphism $V\to T$ is affine. Each inverse image is quasi-compact by the affine-scheme qcqs lemma. For any open cover of $V$, select finitely many members covering each of these finitely many pieces; their union is a finite subcover of $V$. Thus $V$ is quasi-compact. The covering base-change lemma makes $V\to U$ surjective etale; applying the same atlas criterion to $U$ proves it quasi-compact.

source.place: Tag 03E4 (lemma-quasi-compact-space), with definition-quasi-compact, for the qc scheme-atlas criterion; finite pullback and finite affine cover argument

proof.text: Let $R=U\times_XU$, a scheme because the diagonal of $X$ is representable. Its projection $R\to U$ is finite, being a scheme base change of $f$, hence proper and separated by the finite-proper lemma. The relative diagonal $\delta:U\to R$ is a section of this projection, so the section lemma makes it a closed immersion. The map $R\to U\times_KU$ is the scheme test of $\Delta_{X/K}$ along $U\times_KU\to X\times_KX$, hence is a closed immersion by the hypothesis that $X$ is separated over $K$. Composing these scheme closed immersions gives $\Delta_{U/K}$, so $U$ is separated over $K$. Together with local Noetherianness and quasi-compactness already established, $U$ is a Noetherian scheme. (In the algebraic-space convention requiring quasi-separatedness explicitly, it follows here from separatedness over the affine base.) The $K$-morphism $f$ constructed above is finite and surjective, which proves the item.
